scenes.narration: From Jenkins to GitHub Actions. Chapter four: run the converted pipeline on real GitHub, first for free, then on GitHub's own machines.
onScreen: Chapter four: self-hosted runners, then GitHub-hosted runners

scenes.narration: A quick note on what this chapter is. Everything so far ran on this machine. Here the converted workflow runs on GitHub itself, in a private test repository, once for each kind of runner. The terminal output is replayed from those real runs, with the account and repository names hidden. One earlier self-hosted run was also filmed live, sped up, with the account name and IDs masked. It assumes the earlier chapters are done. The hosted run spent real Actions minutes, and each command was run once.

data.foot: A match here is encouraging evidence for one example. It is not proof the migration is ready for production.

scenes.narration: A runner is the machine that carries out a workflow's jobs. Self-hosted runners are ones you provide. Here they are short-lived containers on this machine, which GitHub does not bill for. GitHub-hosted runners are GitHub's own machines, and on a private repository their time is counted against your monthly allowance.

onScreen.v: Temporary runner containers started on this machine; no billable minutes
GitHub's own machines; billed per job, at least one minute each
The converted workflow, the same eleven jobs, either way
Compare the steps that ran with what Jenkins did

scenes.narration: Each run follows the same path. The harness pushes a temporary branch to the test repository. GitHub starts the workflow. For self-hosted runs, the harness starts one runner container per job. When it finishes, the harness downloads the logs, compares them with Jenkins, and deletes the branch.

scenes.source: README 7.1 command and Expected; capture run-selfhosted #0

beats.narration: One command, about two minutes. It pushes the branch, starts eleven runners, one for each job, and reports the result. Look for the billable minutes, and the verdict at the bottom.

highlight.text: success: forty-one trace events, zero billable minutes

beats.narration: The harness saves a record of the run. These are the eleven jobs: the build, three quality checks, three compatibility cells, publish, the deploy gate, deploy and the final post job. All succeeded, on self-hosted runners.

highlight.text: Label self-hosted: ran on the local runners

scenes.narration: This is the same run on GitHub's own web page. The run graph shows the eleven jobs in order, with the three compatibility cells grouped as a matrix, and the deploy gate just before Deploy. It took one minute forty-nine seconds, and everything is green. It is the counterpart of the Jenkins stage view in chapter one.

annotations.label: The run graph: eleven jobs, the matrix grouped

scenes.narration: Opening one job shows its steps. Here are the unit tests. One step prints a marker line: the stage name and the kind of step. Jenkins printed the same markers in chapter three, and these lines are what the harness compares.

annotations.label: The trace marker, as on the Jenkins console
The stage-entry step that evaluates the condition

scenes.narration: And this is another self-hosted trace run of the same example, filmed live the day before, and sped up seven times. The jobs turn green as they finish: publish, then the gate job, Deploy when, then Deploy and the post job. All eleven succeed, in one minute forty-three seconds.

scenes.source: README 7.1 optional full run; capture run-selfhosted-full #0

beats.narration: The optional second run uses full mode: the real commands run on GitHub, not just markers. It took about three minutes, still zero billable minutes. The verdict reads equivalent.

scenes.source: shots/03-selfhosted-full-graph.png; README Part 7.1 optional full run
scenes.narration: The full run on the same page. It took two minutes forty-seven seconds and uploaded seventeen artifacts. Below the graph, the unit test job's own summary reports five tests, no failures, no errors, none skipped.

scenes.source: README 7.1 artifacts list; capture local-checks #2 and #3 (from the run log)
scenes.part: Part 7.1 · what the full run uploaded

beats.narration: The run's log shows what it uploaded: the release, the deploy record, test reports, stashes, and six workspace hand-offs. Seventeen artifacts. The numbers in the names change from run to run, and this list comes from the log, not the run page.

highlight.text: Numbers vary per run: forty-one and forty-seven here

scenes.narration: Scrolling to the bottom of the run page lists the artifacts the full run uploaded. There are seventeen: the stashes, the test reports, the report page, and six that hand the workspace from job to job. This is the same list the log showed, now in the interface.

annotations.label: Seventeen artifacts, as in the log

beats.narration: Now the part that costs money. First, check the allowance. One hundred and forty-four of three thousand minutes used this month. The usage data is complete, read from GitHub's billing data, so the guard decides on real figures.

highlight.text: Usage data: complete, from the billing API

scenes.source: README 7.2 paragraph on jobs, minutes and the cap; capture run-hosted (ALLOW line)
scenes.narration: Here is the reasoning. The workflow now has eleven jobs, each billed for at least one minute, so about eleven minutes. The guard plans for the worst case, fifty-five minutes. The guide's cap of fifty refused that, so the cap was raised to sixty for this one run.

beats.narration: The hosted run. The guard allows it and reserves fifty-five minutes, the worst case. The run succeeds with eleven billable minutes. The verdict is equivalent, one hundred percent.

highlight.text: Reserved fifty-five minutes as the worst case

beats.narration: The saved record shows why. The run took about a minute, but there are eleven jobs, each rounded up to a whole minute. The same eleven jobs as before, now on GitHub's own machines.

highlight.text: Eleven jobs on GitHub's ubuntu runners
About a minute of wall-clock time, eleven billed minutes

scenes.narration: And the hosted run on GitHub's web page. Same eleven jobs, same graph, finished in fifty-two seconds. The notices below mention the ubuntu-latest label, which shows these jobs ran on GitHub's own machines.

beats.narration: Check the allowance again. Used minutes went from one hundred and forty-four to one hundred and fifty-five: the eleven minutes. The harness ledger counts eleven hosted runs this month, seventy-five billable minutes in all.

highlight.text: 144 to 155 minutes used: the eleven minutes
Ledger: eleven hosted runs this month, 75 minutes

scenes.source: README 'Where the results are'; capture gh-runs #0

beats.narration: The runs also stay on GitHub. This read-only listing, trimmed to the result and the title, shows the five most recent. Each title names the tier and the example. All five succeeded.

scenes.narration: Side by side. All three runs succeeded and matched Jenkins. The two self-hosted runs cost no billable minutes. The hosted run cost eleven, even though it was the quickest. Timings come from this one machine and this one day.

scenes.title: Chapter four: real GitHub Actions
scenes.narration: To recap. The converted workflow ran on GitHub with self-hosted runners at no cost, and on GitHub-hosted runners for eleven billable minutes. Both matched Jenkins in trace mode. The caveats. This is one example, run once per kind, in a private test repository. The guard's cap was raised for the one hosted run. This does not prove the migration is ready for production.
